new mexico.period1_limits: $50,000 per person / $100,000 per incident bodily injury and death, $25,000 property damage
new mexico.period2_3_limits: $1,000,000 primary automobile liability for death, bodily injury and property damage
new mexico.sol_note: The clock starts on the date of the crash, is paused for minors until they turn 18, and a claim against a government entity faces a much shorter 90-day notice deadline under the New Mexico Tort Claims Act.
new mexico.sources: NMSA 1978 Section 65-7-8 (Justia), Transportation Network Company Services Act (nmlegis.gov), 18.7.1 NMAC (srca.nm.gov), NMSA 1978 Section 37-1-8
new mexico.state_note: Regulation of TNCs moved from the Public Regulation Commission to the Department of Transportation on July 1, 2024, under the current version of 18.7.1 NMAC.
new mexico.tnc_statute: Transportation Network Company Services Act, NMSA 1978 Sections 65-7-1 to 65-7-22 (insurance requirements at Section 65-7-8)
new mexico.um_uim_note: UM/UIM coverage is required to the extent required by NMSA 1978 Section 66-5-301, which requires insurers to offer uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage equal to the bodily injury limits; it applies in both Period 1 and during a prearranged ride unless the driver rejected it in writing.
new mexico.who_pays_note: While the app is off, only the driver's personal auto policy pays. Once the driver is logged on, the driver or the TNC must maintain primary coverage that recognizes rideshare use, and Uber/Lyft provide contingent coverage in Period 1 and the $1,000,000 policy once a ride is accepted. If the driver's personal policy has lapsed or does not provide the required coverage, the TNC's insurance steps in as the primary coverage, and New Mexico law expressly allows personal auto insurers to exclude coverage while the car is used for rideshare.

new york.agency_name: New York State Department of Financial Services
new york.period1_limits: $75,000 per person / $150,000 per accident bodily injury or death, $25,000 property damage, plus uninsured motorist coverage and personal injury protection (no-fault)
new york.period2_3_limits: $1,250,000 liability for bodily injury, death and property damage, plus $1,250,000 supplemental uninsured/underinsured motorist (SUM) coverage and personal injury protection (no-fault)
new york.sol_note: The clock starts on the date of the crash, but a no-fault (PIP) claim must be filed within 30 days of the crash, and a claim against a city or other government body requires a notice of claim within 90 days.
new york.sources: NY Vehicle and Traffic Law Section 1693, NY Department of Financial Services TNC FAQ (dfs.ny.gov), CPLR Section 214
new york.state_note: New York's limits are the highest in this group outside New York City ($1,250,000 per trip), but Article 44-B does not apply to trips originating in New York City, where Uber and Lyft cars are for-hire vehicles under Taxi and Limousine Commission (TLC) rules requiring at least $100,000/$300,000 bodily injury coverage.
new york.tnc_statute: Vehicle and Traffic Law Article 44-B, Transportation Network Company Services, Sections 1691-1699 (insurance requirements at Section 1693)
new york.um_uim_note: Uninsured motorist coverage is required in Period 1, and during a prearranged trip the policy must include $1,250,000 in supplemental uninsured/underinsured motorist (SUM) coverage — far above the $25,000 minimum UM coverage on a regular New York auto policy.
new york.who_pays_note: With the app off, only the driver's personal auto policy pays, at New York's $25,000/$50,000 minimums plus $50,000 no-fault PIP. Once logged on, the TNC must maintain a group policy that satisfies the limits above, and that TNC coverage is primary; a personal insurer's rideshare exclusion does not defeat the TNC coverage. No-fault PIP pays medical bills and lost wages first regardless of fault, and a claim for pain and suffering still requires a 'serious injury' under Insurance Law Section 5102(d).

north carolina.agency_name: North Carolina Division of Motor Vehicles
north carolina.period1_limits: $50,000 per person / $100,000 per accident bodily injury, $25,000 property damage
north carolina.period2_3_limits: $1,000,000 primary liability for death, bodily injury and property damage
north carolina.sol_note: The clock starts on the date of the crash, or when a hidden injury is or should have been discovered, with a 10-year outer limit; the period is paused while the injured person is a minor.
north carolina.sources: N.C.G.S. Sections 20-280.3 and 20-280.4 (ncleg.gov), N.C.G.S. Section 1-52, NC Division of Motor Vehicles TNC permit packet (ncshp.gov)
north carolina.state_note: North Carolina is one of the few states that still uses contributory negligence, so any fault on the injured person's part, no matter how small, can bar recovery entirely. TNCs must get a permit from the Division of Motor Vehicles and renew it annually.
north carolina.tnc_statute: Transportation Network Companies Act, N.C.G.S. Article 10A, Sections 20-280.1 to 20-280.10 (insurance requirements at Section 20-280.4)
north carolina.um_uim_note: Uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage is required with the TNC policy under North Carolina's mandatory UM law; during Periods 2-3 Uber and Lyft carry $1,000,000 in UM/UIM coverage, and in Period 1 UM/UIM follows the state's mandatory uninsured motorist requirements.
north carolina.who_pays_note: With the app off, only the driver's personal auto policy pays. In Period 1, Uber and Lyft provide contingent liability coverage that only pays if the driver's personal policy denies the claim or is exhausted, which is where most coverage disputes arise. Once a ride is accepted, the TNC's $1,000,000 policy is primary, and the driver's personal insurer may exclude rideshare use entirely.

north dakota.period1_limits: $50,000 per person / $100,000 per accident bodily injury, $25,000 property damage
north dakota.period2_3_limits: $1,000,000 primary liability for death, bodily injury and property damage
north dakota.sol_note: The clock starts on the date of the crash and is paused for minors until age 18, but a wrongful-death claim has a shorter 2-year deadline.
north dakota.sources: N.D.C.C. Chapters 39-34 and 26.1-40.1, 2023 HB 1440 (ndlegis.gov), N.D.C.C. Section 28-01-16(5)
north dakota.state_note: North Dakota's 6-year personal injury deadline is among the longest in the country, and its no-fault PIP system means medical bills are paid through PIP regardless of fault. TNCs and drivers are governed exclusively by Chapters 39-34 and 26.1-40.1, and cities may not add their own TNC rules.
north dakota.tnc_statute: Transportation Company Networks, N.D.C.C. Chapter 39-34, and TNC insurance, N.D.C.C. Chapter 26.1-40.1 (Sections 26.1-40.1-03 and 26.1-40.1-04), as amended by 2023 HB 1440
north dakota.um_uim_note: UM and UIM coverage must meet the requirements of N.D.C.C. Sections 26.1-40-15.2 and 26.1-40-15.3 and is primary coverage during an engaged or on-board ride; personal injury protection (PIP) under Chapter 26.1-41 is also required for drivers, passengers and pedestrians.
north dakota.who_pays_note: With the app off, only the driver's personal auto policy pays. Once logged on, the TNC or the driver must maintain TNC insurance, and the $1,000,000 policy is primary once a ride is accepted. Under a 2023 change, TNC coverage may not depend on the driver's personal insurer first denying the claim, and if the personal policy does not cover the loss the TNC policy pays from the first dollar.

ohio.period1_limits: $50,000 per person / $100,000 per accident bodily injury or death, $25,000 property damage
ohio.period2_3_limits: $1,000,000 primary liability for bodily injury or death and property damage in any one accident
ohio.sol_note: The clock starts on the date of the crash, is paused for minors until they turn 18, and a claim involving a government vehicle usually requires prompt notice and faces shorter deadlines.
ohio.sources: Ohio Revised Code Sections 3942.02, 4925.02 and 4925.10 (codes.ohio.gov), Ohio Revised Code Section 2305.10(A)
ohio.state_note: Ohio law makes TNCs pay and defend claims when a driver fails to maintain the required coverage, and drivers are independent contractors, not employees, under Ohio Revised Code Section 4925.10, so the TNC generally cannot be sued under respondeat superior for a driver's negligence.
ohio.tnc_statute: Ohio Revised Code Chapter 4925 (Transportation Network Companies) and Chapter 3942 (TNC insurance, Section 3942.02)
ohio.um_uim_note: UM/UIM coverage is not required by Ohio law — it is optional in Ohio and the TNC statute does not mandate it — though Uber's and Lyft's own $1,000,000 policies include uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage during Periods 2-3.
ohio.who_pays_note: With the app off, only the driver's personal auto policy pays, at Ohio's $25,000/$50,000/$25,000 minimums. Once logged on, the driver or the TNC must maintain primary coverage that recognizes rideshare use, with Uber/Lyft providing contingent coverage in Period 1 and the $1,000,000 policy once a ride is accepted. If the driver's personal policy does not provide the required coverage, the TNC's insurance must provide it from the first dollar, and the TNC may not require the personal insurer to deny the claim first; personal insurers may exclude all coverage while the driver is logged on.

oklahoma.period1_limits: $50,000 per person / $100,000 per incident bodily injury and death, $25,000 property damage
oklahoma.period2_3_limits: $1,000,000 primary liability for death, bodily injury and property damage
oklahoma.sol_note: The clock starts on the date of the crash (or when the injury is discovered); minors get extra time, and a claim involving a government vehicle requires a written notice to the government within 1 year under the Governmental Tort Claims Act.
oklahoma.sources: 47 O.S. Section 1025 (oklegislature.gov), Oklahoma Transportation Network Company Services Act 47 O.S. Sections 1010-1030, 12 O.S. Section 95(A)(3)
oklahoma.state_note: A bill introduced in the 2026 session (HB 4357) would double the Period 1 minimums to $100,000 per person / $200,000 per incident / $50,000 property damage, but it has not passed, so the $50,000/$100,000/$25,000 limits remain the law.
oklahoma.tnc_statute: Oklahoma Transportation Network Company Services Act, 47 O.S. Sections 1010-1030 (insurance requirements at Section 1025)
oklahoma.um_uim_note: Uninsured motorist coverage is required in both Period 1 and during a prearranged ride unless the driver waived it in writing under 36 O.S. Section 3636; the minimum UM limits track Oklahoma's $25,000 per person / $50,000 per accident minimums.
oklahoma.who_pays_note: With the app off, only the driver's personal auto policy pays, at Oklahoma's $25,000/$50,000/$25,000 minimums. Once logged on, the driver or the TNC must maintain primary coverage that recognizes rideshare use, with the platform's policy covering Period 1 and the $1,000,000 policy once a ride is accepted. If the driver's personal policy has lapsed or does not provide the required coverage, the TNC's insurance provides it from the first dollar, and personal auto policies typically exclude liability while carrying passengers for a fee.

oregon.agency_name: Portland Bureau of Transportation (Private For-Hire Transportation program)
oregon.period1_limits: $50,000 per person / $100,000 per incident bodily injury and death, $25,000 property damage (Portland City Code Section 16.40.230; no statewide tiered minimum exists)
oregon.period2_3_limits: $1,000,000 combined single limit primary liability (Portland City Code Section 16.40.230; no statewide tiered minimum exists)
oregon.sol_note: The clock starts on the date of the crash or when the injury is discovered, with a 10-year outer limit under ORS 12.115; a claim against a government body needs a tort-claim notice within 180 days.
oregon.sources: ORS 742.518, 742.520 and 742.502, Portland City Code Sections 16.40.230 and 16.40.010 (portland.gov), ORS 12.110(1)
oregon.state_note: Oregon is unusual in having no comprehensive statewide TNC law: the only statewide TNC-specific statute requires PIP benefits, and permits, background checks and the $50,000/$100,000/$25,000 and $1,000,000 insurance tiers are set by individual cities, with Portland's Chapter 16.40 as the model. Oregon uses modified comparative fault with a 51% bar under ORS 31.600.
oregon.tnc_statute: Oregon Revised Statutes Sections 742.518 and 742.520 (TNC personal injury protection, HB 2393 of 2021); Portland City Code Chapter 16.40, Section 16.40.230 (insurance tiers) — Oregon has no statewide TNC operating statute
oregon.um_uim_note: Oregon law (ORS 742.502) requires UM/UIM coverage equal to the bodily injury liability limits on every auto policy, including TNC coverage; the statewide TNC law also requires personal injury protection of at least $15,000 in medical expenses plus up to $3,000 per month in wage loss for up to 52 weeks for drivers, passengers and pedestrians struck by the vehicle.
oregon.who_pays_note: With the app off, only the driver's personal auto policy pays. In Portland, the TNC must maintain primary coverage for all periods, with the $50,000/$100,000/$25,000 tier while waiting and $1,000,000 once a ride is accepted, so there is no coverage gap. Outside Portland there is no statewide tiered liability law, so coverage depends on the city, the TNC's own policy, and whether the driver's personal policy has a livery exclusion, which can leave a gap in Period 1.

pennsylvania.period1_limits: $50,000 per person / $100,000 per incident death and bodily injury, $25,000 property damage, plus first-party medical benefits of $25,000 for pedestrians and $5,000 for the driver
pennsylvania.period2_3_limits: $500,000 primary automobile liability for death, bodily injury and property damage, plus first-party medical benefits of $25,000 for passengers and pedestrians
pennsylvania.sol_note: The clock starts on the date of the crash or when the injury is discovered; minors have until 2 years after turning 18, and a claim against a government body needs written notice within 6 months.
pennsylvania.sources: 66 Pa.C.S. Section 2603.1 (legis.state.pa.us), 53 Pa.C.S. Section 57A07, PA PUC TNC page (puc.pa.gov), 42 Pa.C.S. Section 5524(2)
pennsylvania.state_note: Pennsylvania's statutory trip minimum is only $500,000, not $1,000,000 as many secondary sources claim — the $1,000,000 figure is the companies' own policy limit, not the state floor. Chapter 26 does not apply inside a city of the first class, so rides in Philadelphia are regulated by the Philadelphia Parking Authority under 53 Pa.C.S. Chapter 57A.
pennsylvania.tnc_statute: Transportation Network Service, 66 Pa.C.S. Chapter 26, Sections 2601-2605 (insurance requirements at Section 2603.1); Philadelphia is governed separately by 53 Pa.C.S. Chapter 57A, Section 57A07
pennsylvania.um_uim_note: UM/UIM coverage is not required by Pennsylvania law — it is optional and the TNC statute does not require it — though Uber's and Lyft's own policies typically include UM/UIM coverage during a trip; the $500,000 statutory trip minimum is lower than the companies' own $1,000,000 policies.
pennsylvania.who_pays_note: With the app off, only the driver's personal auto policy pays, at Pennsylvania's $15,000/$30,000 minimums. Once logged on, the driver or the TNC must maintain primary coverage that recognizes rideshare use, and the TNC's coverage does not depend on the personal insurer denying the claim first. If the driver's policy has lapsed or does not provide the required coverage, the TNC's insurance provides it from the first dollar and its insurer has the duty to defend the claim.

rhode island.agency_name: Rhode Island Division of Public Utilities and Carriers
rhode island.period1_limits: $50,000 per person / $100,000 per incident death and bodily injury, $25,000 property damage
rhode island.period2_3_limits: $1,500,000 primary automobile liability for death, bodily injury and property damage
rhode island.sol_note: The clock starts on the date of the crash or when the injury is discovered; the period is paused for minors, and a claim against a city or town must first be presented to the municipality on a much shorter deadline.
rhode island.sources: R.I. Gen. Laws Section 39-14.2-14 (law.justia.com), R.I. Gen. Laws Chapter 39-14.2, 815-RICR-50-10-5, R.I. Gen. Laws Section 9-1-14(b)
rhode island.state_note: Rhode Island's $1,500,000 trip minimum is the highest in this group — 50% above the usual $1,000,000 — and the Division of Public Utilities and Carriers also requires TNCs to cap surge pricing during disasters and states of emergency.
rhode island.tnc_statute: Transportation Network Company Services, R.I. Gen. Laws Chapter 39-14.2 (insurance requirements at Section 39-14.2-14)
rhode island.um_uim_note: UM/UIM coverage is required in both Period 1 and during prearranged rides to the extent required by R.I. Gen. Laws Section 27-7-2.1, at least the state minimum of $25,000 per person / $50,000 per accident.
rhode island.who_pays_note: With the app off, only the driver's personal auto policy pays. Once logged on, the driver or the TNC must maintain primary coverage that recognizes rideshare use, with the TNC's policy covering Period 1 and the $1,500,000 policy once a ride is accepted. If the driver's policy has lapsed or does not provide the required coverage, the TNC's insurance provides it from the first dollar and its insurer has the duty to defend, and TNC coverage may not be made to depend on the personal insurer first denying the claim.

south carolina.agency_name: South Carolina Public Service Commission (with the Office of Regulatory Staff)
south carolina.period1_limits: $50,000 per person / $100,000 per incident bodily injury and death, $50,000 property damage
south carolina.period2_3_limits: $1,000,000 primary automobile liability for death, bodily injury and property damage
south carolina.sol_note: The clock starts on the date of the crash or when the injury is discovered; minors get extra time, and a claim against a government vehicle must go through the South Carolina Tort Claims Act with a 1-year notice deadline.
south carolina.sources: S.C. Code Sections 58-23-1610, 58-23-1625 and 58-23-1630 (law.justia.com), S.C. Code Section 15-3-530(5), SC Office of Regulatory Staff transportation page (ors.sc.gov)
south carolina.state_note: South Carolina's Period 1 property damage minimum is $50,000, double the $25,000 used in most states; some secondary sources wrongly state the per-incident bodily injury limit as $150,000, but the statute (Section 58-23-1630) says $100,000. TNCs need a certificate of public convenience and necessity from the Public Service Commission, and drivers must display a vehicle decal and license plate number visible from the front of the car.
south carolina.tnc_statute: Transportation Network Company Act, S.C. Code Title 58, Chapter 23, Article 16, Sections 58-23-1610 to 58-23-1720 (insurance requirements at Section 58-23-1630)
south carolina.um_uim_note: Uninsured motorist coverage is required in both Period 1 and during a prearranged ride; South Carolina's UM minimum is $25,000 per person / $50,000 per accident bodily injury and $25,000 property damage.
south carolina.who_pays_note: With the app off, only the driver's personal auto policy pays, at South Carolina's $25,000/$50,000/$25,000 minimums. Once logged on, the driver or the TNC must maintain primary coverage that recognizes rideshare use, with the platform's contingent policy covering Period 1 and the $1,000,000 policy once a ride is accepted. South Carolina law expressly excludes the driver's personal policy while the driver is logged on or providing a prearranged ride, so the TNC policy is the one that pays during those periods.
